result:
There's a particular pleasure in being told to write about anything, which is immediately followed by a particular vertigo. Anything is too much. The blank page isn't blank so much as infinitely crowded—every possible subject pressing against the glass. So let me start with something small and see where it goes: the word "threshold."

I've been thinking about thresholds because they're one of those concepts that does double duty so gracefully you almost don't notice. A threshold is the strip of wood at the bottom of a doorway, the literal thing you step over when entering a house. And it's also the point at which something begins to happen—the threshold of hearing, the threshold of pain, the threshold of a new era. The metaphor is so old it's fossilized. We don't hear the doorway in it anymore. But once you do hear it, you can't stop: every time someone says "we're on the threshold of a breakthrough," there's a ghost of a foot lifting over a wooden beam, a body passing from one room into another.

Language is full of these buried buildings. "Consider" may carry the stars in it—con-siderare, possibly from sidus, to examine the stars together, the way ancient navigators and augurs did. "Companion" holds bread: com-panis, the one you share bread with. "Disaster" is a bad star. We speak in ruins. Every sentence is an archaeological site, and most of the time we walk across it like commuters over Roman roads, never wondering what's underneath the asphalt.

I find this consoling, somehow. It suggests that meaning is never invented from scratch—it's inherited, repurposed, squatted in. When you reach for a word to describe something new, you're handed a tool that was shaped by people solving entirely different problems, and you make it work anyway. The history of language is a history of making-do, of approximation, of metaphors stretched until they snap and become literal. "Broadcast" used to mean scattering seeds by hand across a field. Then radio came, and we needed a word for flinging invisible voices across the countryside, and there it was, waiting.

This makes me wonder about the words we're stretching right now. "Stream" used to be water; now it's video. "Cloud" used to be weather; now it's someone else's computer. "Feed" used to be what you gave animals; now it's what algorithms give you, which—the more you sit with that one, the less comfortable it gets. The metaphors we choose end up choosing things for us. If your information arrives as a "feed," you're positioned as livestock at a trough. If it arrived as a "library" or a "garden" or a "conversation," maybe you'd behave differently. Maybe you'd browse instead of graze.

There's a school of thought—Lakoff and Johnson are the famous names—arguing that metaphor isn't decoration but the basic structure of how we think. We understand time as space (the future is "ahead," the past is "behind"), argument as war ("he attacked my position," "her claims are indefensible"), ideas as objects ("let me give you a thought"). Strip away the metaphors and there's almost nothing left to think with. The mind is a building made of borrowed bricks.

If that's true, it raises a question I find genuinely hard: can you have a thought your language doesn't have furniture for? People who speak languages with absolute directions instead of relative ones—where you'd say "the cup is to your north" rather than "to your left"—maintain a kind of constant internal compass that speakers of English mostly lack. The language doesn't just describe their orientation; it trains it. That's not quite the strong claim that language imprisons thought, which has been debunked in its cartoonish forms. But it's the softer, stranger claim that language is a set of habits, and habits are destiny in slow motion.

Let me circle back to thresholds, because I promised myself I would wander but not get lost. There's a concept in anthropology—liminality, from limen, the Latin for threshold—describing the state of being between. The initiate who is no longer a child but not yet an adult. The traveler in the airport, who is legally and emotionally nowhere. The hour of dusk, which is neither day nor night. Anthropologists noticed that cultures treat these in-between states with enormous care: they're dangerous, sacred, charged. Things that don't fit categories make us nervous, and so we surround them with ritual, the way you'd pack something fragile.

I suspect a lot of modern unease is liminal unease. We're between media regimes, between climate eras, between ideas of work, between versions of ourselves that update faster than we can integrate them. The old anthropological wisdom would say: of course this feels destabilizing—you're standing in a doorway, and doorways are where the wind comes through. The mistake is thinking the doorway is a destination. Nobody is supposed to live on the threshold. You're supposed to cross.

But crossing requires knowing which room you're trying to enter, and that's the part that's genuinely unclear, for individuals and civilizations alike. Maybe that's why the etymology comforts me. The threshold, as an object, is humble. It's a worn piece of wood. Thousands of feet have crossed it. It exists precisely because crossing is ordinary—because people pass between rooms all day, every day, without ceremony. The grand metaphorical threshold and the mundane physical one are the same word because, at some level, they're the same act. You lift your foot. You put it down somewhere new. The room you enter is never quite the room you imagined from the other side, and you adjust, the way you always have.

I started with vertigo at the blank page and I've ended up at a doorway, which feels right. Writing freely turns out to mean writing across—from one half-formed idea to the next, trusting that the floor continues on the other side. Usually it does. And when it doesn't, well: "disaster" is just a bad star, and stars move, and tomorrow you consider them again.
